props.title: Dark Water

sections.content: Dark Water stands as a haunting example of Hollywood remaking Asian horror, following the success of The Ring (2002). Based on Koji Suzuki's novel and Hideo Nakata's 2002 Japanese film, the American version stars Jennifer Connelly as a mother fighting for custody while facing supernatural occurrences in a dilapidated apartment building. The film taps into primal fears about motherhood and urban decay, similar to psychological horror masterpieces like Rosemary's Baby (1968) and The Babadook (2014).

sections.content: Director Walter Salles brings his arthouse sensibilities to Dark Water, emphasizing atmospheric dread over jump scares. The film's waterlogged aesthetics and decaying urban setting echo similar themes in Session 9 (2001) and 1408 (2007), where architecture itself becomes a character. The constant presence of water - dripping, flooding, seeping - creates a suffocating atmosphere that mirrors the protagonist's psychological deterioration.

The film's exploration of maternal anxiety aligns it with other psychological horror films like The Sixth Sense (1999) and The Orphanage (2007). Connelly's performance as Dahlia Williams captures the desperation of a mother trying to protect her child while questioning her own sanity, reminiscent of Nicole Kidman's work in The Others (2001). sections.content: Dark Water emerged during a significant period of Asian horror remakes, including The Grudge (2004), Pulse (2006), and The Eye (2008). While many of these adaptations struggled to capture the subtle psychological terror of their sources, Dark Water succeeded by emphasizing emotional depth over spectacle, similar to Gore Verbinski's approach with The Ring (2002).
